storm.summary_layperson: No storms anywhere nearby today — a cool, quiet autumn day under high pressure, with nothing on radar and no warnings.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No marine-layer buffer today: the Sound (65°F) is warmer than the morning air, and even at the afternoon high the air only gets about 1°F above the water — never near the ~5°F needed — so the Sound isn't shaping the weather either way.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture: Strong high pressure (about 1030 hPa) sits over southern New England this morning. Radar from Upton (KOKX) shows no echoes to track, there are no NWS watches, warnings, or advisories, and the atmosphere has zero instability (0 J/kg of CAPE, the fuel thunderstorms need). The upper-level winds are fairly strong (about 41 kt of shear), but with no instability there is nothing for that wind to organize.

Local modifier: On summer days the cool Sound often acts as a shield — when the air over land is much warmer than the water, a stable, cool layer forms near the surface that chokes storms. Today the setup is reversed: the Sound is about 65°F while the air at the cove was about 55°F at 8:40 AM. The model warms the air to about 66°F by midday, so the air–water gap only reaches roughly +1°F around noon to 4 PM before falling back below the water temperature after sunset (6:21 PM). It never approaches the ~5°F threshold, so there is no protective marine layer at any point today — but there is also nothing for it to protect against.

Most likely outcome: Dry for the cove and the surrounding towns alike. Expect partly sunny skies and a high in the mid-60s. The forecasters' discussion points to the next shower chance arriving late Tuesday into Wednesday, with an isolated thunderstorm possible then.

What would change the call: Not much today. Only an unexpected disturbance producing instability could do it, and nothing in the model run (zero instability through 7 PM) or the forecaster discussion points that way.

wind.tactics_blurb: A light easterly drifter day with no sea breeze to rescue it — the wind swings from NE in the late morning to ESE after 1 PM. Once it's ESE, favor the right (south/west) side, away from Greenwich Point's wind shadow, and hold off racing until it settles.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Regime call — light gradient wind, no sea breeze. A sea breeze needs the land to heat well above the water (at least ~5°F). Today it can't: the Sound is about 65°F and the air at Riverside YC was 54.7°F at 8:40 AM. The model peaks the air near 66°F around noon to 4 PM, an air–water temperature difference of only about 1°F. No coastal or inland station is showing southerly flow (0 of 20 coastal stations), so the thermal never gets going. What wind there is comes from the large-scale (gradient) flow around the high, and that's weak: well-sited anemometers average under 2 kt right now, and the cove is effectively calm (RYC 10-minute average 0.3 kt).

Through the window: The model fills in a light NE of about 4–5 kt by 10–11 AM, then rotates it clockwise through ENE at noon to ESE (~105–112°) at 6–7 kt from 1 to 3 PM, which is the best wind of the window. The NWS forecast (east wind around 5 mph) agrees with the easterly call. This is a slow rotation of the background flow around the high, not a sea breeze. It will feel like a steady drift to the right through midday rather than shifts you can play back and forth.

Where the pressure is: In the morning NE, flow comes off the land cleanly and is fairly uniform, with a touch more pressure mid-cove. Once it goes ESE, Greenwich Point (Tod's Point) sits upwind of the east side of the course and throws a wind shadow. Pressure favors the west and south side — the right side on an ESE beat — while the shore near Tod's Point stays lighter and patchier. A light easterly is one of the cove's softest directions, so the open Sound may look breezier than the start line feels.

Shift character: A persistent clockwise swing from 10 AM to about 1 PM (NE → ESE, about 75°), then roughly steady ESE, beginning to back slightly by 3 PM. During the swing, the side the wind is rotating toward pays. In the settled ESE, puffs will be patchy at this strength rather than cleanly oscillating.

What racers will feel: 4–5 kt before noon is drifter territory — dinghies can move, keelboats will struggle, and postponement on shore or on the water until the easterly settles is a real possibility. 6–7 kt from 1 to 3 PM is raceable light air for most fleets. Treat the 2–3 PM numbers with some caution: they come from the model's lower-confidence later hours. Gusts are estimated (the model output doesn't include them).

data_caveats: Buoy 44040 (western Sound) stale — last reading 174 min ago; its water-temperature feed also failed (404), so Sound water temperature comes from Bridgeport Harbor (BRHC3)
Marine-layer trend uses raw model air temperatures (pipeline found no current inland air-temp reading); RYC's live 54.7°F is consistent with the model's morning values
2–3 PM wind numbers come from the model's lower-confidence later hours (f07–f08)
Gust values are estimated — the model wind output for this window has no gust field
